title: Root lnd ExecStartPost writes/chowns through attacker-controlled symlinks in lnd-owned /run/lnd
attack_scenario: Attacker with code execution as the lnd user (remote lnd RCE). RuntimeDirectory /run/lnd is owned by lnd (mode 711), so the attacker replaces /run/lnd/btcpayserver.macaroon with a symlink to an arbitrary root-owned path, then crashes lnd; Restart=on-failure re-runs ExecStartPost. That command is nbLib.rootScript, i.e. prefixed with '+' (pkgs/lib.nix:88), so it runs as root with User= AND all sandboxing (ProtectSystem=strict etc.) lifted. The shell redirect '> $macaroonPath' follows the symlink and truncates/writes the target as root (arbitrary file clobber: /etc/passwd, /etc/nix-bitcoin-secrets/lnd-wallet-password, bitcoind state, backups), and 'chown user:' without -h chowns the symlink target to the macaroon's configured user (btcpayserver), handing a network-facing service user ownership of an arbitrary file. Payoff: node destruction / funds-lockout DoS beyond the service sandbox, and a chown primitive that chains with a btcpayserver compromise to full file access.
impact: dos (node/funds destruction as root) + privesc primitive chained via arbitrary chown; breaches the sandbox boundary the hardening is meant to enforce
false_positive_risk: Mechanism verified against systemd semantics ('+' disables sandboxing; RuntimeDirectory owned by service User). Content written is an uncontrolled random macaroon, so direct RCE is not possible — impact is clobber/chown, hence medium not high. If cfg.macaroons is empty (no btcpayserver lnd backend) the loop body never runs.
recommendation: Don't write as root into a service-owned directory. Write via install(1) which unlinks the destination first (e.g. 'install -m 440 -o <user> /dev/stdin "$macaroonPath"'), or set RuntimeDirectory ownership to root (RuntimeDirectoryMode with a root-owned dir and group-readable files), or add 'chown -h' and an explicit 'test ! -L' guard mirroring the onion-addresses M-4 fix.

title: btcpayserver-reachable bitcoind RPC user retains setban, enabling peer-eclipse from a web-app compromise
attack_scenario: Attacker remotely compromises btcpayserver (internet-facing .NET app; the class has had critical auth-bypass CVEs, e.g. the 2.4.2 macaroon-theft advisory). The btcpayserver user is in group nbxplorer (btcpayserver.nix:237 extraGroups), and the secret 'bitcoin-rpcpassword-btcpayserver' is group nbxplorer mode 440 under the 0751-traversable secretsDir, so the attacker reads the RPC password. In the default non-netns layout the attacker then calls bitcoind RPC on 127.0.0.1:8332 and uses whitelisted 'setban' to ban every honest peer reported by whitelisted 'getpeerinfo'/'getnodeaddresses' (long bantime, subnets), while the attacker's Sybil peers on the network absorb the freed slots. With bitcoind eclipsed, the attacker feeds a fake chain to nbxplorer/btcpayserver and double-spends on-chain payments the merchant accepts as confirmed; lnd's on-chain view degrades too. Payoff: funds (payment fraud) / dos.
impact: funds (double-spend of accepted on-chain payments) and privacy/dos via peer manipulation; needs the btcpayserver-RCE precondition plus Sybil peers
false_positive_risk: setban may be required by nbxplorer's node-management behavior (grant is inherited from upstream, and the fork deliberately curated this whitelist in 9b73b2d/dd7582f), so removing it might break an nbxplorer feature — needs verification against NBXplorer source. Full eclipse is nontrivial against bitcoind's outbound-peer eviction and anchors; netns-isolation mode blocks btcpayserver->bitcoind RPC at the netns firewall, limiting the scenario to nbxplorer compromise there.
recommendation: Drop 'setban' (and 'generatetoaddress', regtest-only) from the btcpayserver RPC user unless nbxplorer provably needs them; if needed, prefer a dedicated nbxplorer RPC user whose credentials the btcpayserver user cannot read (separate group), so web-app compromise no longer yields P2P-control RPC.

title: onion-addresses: check-then-install TOCTOU on tor-controlled hostname files still allows a root symlink read
evidence:
if [[ -L $src ]]; then
  echo "Error: refusing to read onion hostname via symlink: $src" >&2
  exit 1
fi
install -T -m 400 "$src" "$dst"
attack_scenario: Attacker who has compromised the tor user (controls /var/lib/tor/onion/<svc>/, 0700 tor). The root 'onion-addresses' service (CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE/CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH/CAP_CHOWN) tests '[[ -L $src ]]' and then, in a separate syscall sequence, 'install' opens the same path. By racing a swap of 'hostname' between a regular file and a symlink (e.g. to /etc/shadow or /var/lib/lnd/.../admin.macaroon) across the check/open gap, the attacker gets root to copy the target into /var/lib/onion-addresses/<user>/<svc> with mode 400 owned by an unprivileged user. Payoff: secret exfiltration (macaroon/wallet material) to a low-priv context. Each tor restart grants one attempt window, which bounds reliability.
impact: secrets exfiltration via root read gadget; precondition is tor compromise plus winning a tight race
false_positive_risk: The gap between the -L test and install's open() is microseconds and the service runs once per tor start, so the race may be impractical; the M-4 fix (8c2c342) already closed the non-raced variant and all chowns use -h. May reasonably be considered residual hardening rather than exploitable.
recommendation: Eliminate the check/open gap: open with O_NOFOLLOW (e.g. 'install' from an already-opened fd, or copy via 'cp --no-dereference' + fstat verification), or have tor write hostnames to a root-owned staging dir, or read the hostname with the tor user's privileges instead of root.

title: fork's release tooling and docs still fetch/clone upstream fort-nix/nix-bitcoin, silently discarding fork security fixes
evidence: repo=fort-nix/nix-bitcoin  (also helper/push-release.sh:4 REPO=fort-nix/nix-bitcoin; docs/install.md:213 and examples/README.md:10,21 instruct 'git clone https://github.com/fort-nix/nix-bitcoin' / 'nix run github:fort-nix/nix-bitcoin/release', while README.md:67 uses github:ostermayer/nix-bitcoin/release)
attack_scenario: Not attacker-driven, but a live downgrade channel: a fork user following docs/install.md or running helper/fetch-release 'upgrades' to upstream fort-nix releases. The GPG check passes (pinned key 36C7...0366 is the upstream maintainer's), so nothing warns the user that they have left the fork and redeployed unmaintained upstream code — reintroducing every issue the fork fixed (M-2 lndconnect 0.0.0.0 rebind, M-4 onion symlink, L-8 wireguard root re-exec, trimmed packages' known CVEs such as clboss 0.16.1 fund theft if the user enables those services). Payoff for an opportunistic attacker: users running code with known, documented vulnerabilities who believe they run the hardened fork.
impact: dos/secrets/funds indirectly: silent downgrade to unmaintained upstream that reintroduces known-exploitable modules
false_positive_risk: If the fork intentionally keeps upstream as its release source (push-release.sh also targets fort-nix), this is a deliberate publishing arrangement rather than a bug — but README badges/releases point at ostermayer/nix-bitcoin, indicating the tooling is stale, not intentional.
recommendation: Point helper/fetch-release, helper/push-release.sh, docs/install.md and examples/README.md at the fork's repository and its own signing key; fail loudly if the fetched release's repo/signing identity differs from the fork's.

title: The 'public' bitcoind RPC user is shared by lnd locally and intended for public exposure, so its getpeerinfo/getnodeaddresses leak peer topology and the documented mitigation breaks lnd
evidence:
"getpeerinfo"       # lnd (chain-backend health check), nbxplorer

with lnd.nix:179: `bitcoind.rpcuser=${bitcoind.rpc.users.public.name}` and bitcoind.nix:376 `rpcwhitelist = mkDefault (import ./bitcoind-rpc-public-whitelist.nix);` assigned to rpc.users.public
attack_scenario: The 'public' RPC user exists to be exposed (e.g. via a reverse proxy for a public block explorer or remote client) - that is the whole point of a separately-named public user with a curated whitelist. An attacker holding the public credentials (anyone the operator gave them to, or anyone reaching a proxy that forwards them) calls getpeerinfo and getnodeaddresses and recovers the node's full peer set and advertised addresses, deanonymizing the operator and their peering graph (attacker goal #4). The audit resolution says 'narrow the whitelist in your own config' to mitigate, but because lnd authenticates to bitcoind as this same public user (lnd.conf: bitcoind.rpcuser=public), removing getpeerinfo/getnodeaddresses from the public whitelist also breaks lnd's chain-backend health check. The suggested mitigation is in direct tension with lnd's requirement; the real fix is a separate local-only RPC user for lnd with the topology methods, distinct from the publicly-exposed user.
impact: privacy (peer-topology leak / deanonymization) under the documented public-exposure use case
false_positive_risk: By default the public user is bound to 127.0.0.1 / a netns address and not exposed, so there is no leak without an operator config choice. The maintainers explicitly documented keeping these methods as a deliberate tradeoff (audit M-3 resolution). The finding rests on the premise that exposing this user is an intended use, which the name and whitelist curation support but is not forced.
recommendation: Give lnd its own local RPC user (e.g. rpc.users.lnd) whose whitelist includes getpeerinfo/getnodeaddresses, and keep the 'public' user's whitelist without them so it can be safely exposed. Decouple the local-service credential from the public-facing one.

title: btcpayserver RPC user (used by nbxplorer) is granted setban and generatetoaddress, neither needed, enabling eclipse-DoS of bitcoind if nbxplorer is compromised
attack_scenario: nbxplorer authenticates to bitcoind as the 'btcpayserver' RPC user (nbxplorer settings.config: btcrpcuser=btcpayserver) and, via netns-isolation, is one of the few services with a network path to bitcoind's RPC port. An attacker who compromises nbxplorer (or any holder of the btcpayserver RPC password, which is readable by group nbxplorer = nbxplorer + btcpayserver) gains setban, which nbxplorer never needs for its indexing function. They call `setban 0.0.0.0/0 add` to evict/ban all of bitcoind's peers, eclipsing the node; an eclipsed bitcoind can be fed a false chain view, enabling double-spends of payments btcpayserver already accepted as confirmed, or a plain block-propagation DoS (attacker goals #1/#5). generatetoaddress is mainnet-disabled (regtest only), so it is harmless in production but is still unnecessary surface.
impact: funds (double-spend of accepted btcpayserver payments via eclipse) and DoS, chained on a prior nbxplorer compromise
false_positive_risk: Exploitation requires first compromising nbxplorer, which by default binds only localhost / a netns address and has no public network exposure, so the precondition is itself hard to meet and the incremental risk setban adds over the base nbxplorer compromise is modest. This grant is inherited unchanged from upstream nix-bitcoin (commit 15b574f), not introduced by the fork, though it lives in the fork's in-scope module.
recommendation: Drop setban and generatetoaddress from the btcpayserver RPC user's whitelist (nbxplorer only needs the read-only blockchain/peer-query methods already in the public list). If regtest block generation is needed for tests, grant it only under config.services.bitcoind.regtest.
